name: Allen's Rule
statement: Animals in colder climates tend to have shorter limbs and appendages.
meaning: Warm-blooded animals adapted to cold climates tend to have shorter, thicker limbs, ears, tails, and bills than their relatives in warm climates. Appendages are the body's main heat-exchange surfaces, so their proportions track the temperature of the habitat — stubby in the cold, long and slender in the heat.
mechanism: Extremities have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and are where much heat is exchanged. Short, thick appendages reduce exposed surface and conserve heat in the cold; long, thin, well-vascularised appendages increase surface area to dissipate heat in warmth. It is thermoregulation expressed through the geometry of the body's projecting parts.

examples.text: The Saharan fennec fox has enormous, well-vascularised ears that radiate heat, while the Arctic fox has small, rounded ears that conserve it. A vivid textbook illustration — though as a comparison between two species it is confounded by other differences.
Arctic hares have notably shorter ears than warm-climate jackrabbits, whose long ears help shed heat — the same appendage-length gradient within a familiar group.
Populations native to colder or higher regions tend toward heavier builds and proportionally shorter limbs, though human data are confounded by ancestry, nutrition, and admixture.

variants.name: Bergmann's rule
variants.text: The body-size counterpart: within a related group, colder-climate animals tend to be larger. Allen's rule is often described as complementing it, the two together describing cold-adapted body form.

variants.name: Gloger's rule
variants.text: The pigmentation member of the ecogeographic trio: within a species, more heavily pigmented forms tend to occur in warmer, more humid environments.

whyItMatters: It is one of the classic ecogeographic rules, giving a clean thermoregulatory account of why cold-adapted animals look compact and heat-adapted ones look leggy. Together with Bergmann's and Gloger's rules it forms the standard toolkit for describing how body form varies with climate — with the same caveat that these are tendencies, not laws.

working.text: expect long, thin extremities where heat must be shed and short, thick ones where it must be conserved — the surface-area logic of the rule.

working.lead: Compare within a lineage along a gradient
working.text: the strict pattern is clinal, within a group across a climate gradient; cross-species comparisons like the foxes illustrate but do not rigorously test it.
behaviour, evolutionary history, and body-size scaling can shape appendages independently of climate, so treat conformity as a tendency.

limits: Empirical support is debated, especially at the interspecific level. Nudds and Oswald (2007) argued there is poor empirical support even though it is an established ecological tenet, noting that multi-species studies are confounded by body-size scaling and alternative adaptations. Behaviour, phylogenetic history, and allometry can drive appendage differences independent of climate, and the striking fox-ear example compares different species rather than a clean within-lineage cline. The underlying heat-exchange mechanism is generally supported, but conformity is a tendency with real exceptions, not a deterministic law.
misreadings: It is a statistical tendency, not a law, and its cross-species poster children — like the fennec and Arctic foxes — illustrate the idea without rigorously proving the clinal pattern, since unrelated species differ for many reasons. Appendage length also responds to behaviour and history, not climate alone.
origin: Proposed by the American zoologist Joel Asaph Allen in 1877, in 'The Influence of Physical Conditions in the Genesis of Species', describing how the proportions of limbs and appendages vary with the temperature of an animal's habitat.
